NASA smashed into an asteroid. Now Hera has revealed a strange new world

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (825 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The European Space Agency's (ESA) Hera spacecraft has captured its first close-up image of the Didymos asteroid system, offering scientists a surprising new perspective on the site of NASA's historic asteroid deflection experiment.
  • On September 26, 2022, NASA's DART spacecraft deliberately crashed into Dimorphos, the smaller of the two asteroids in the system.
  • The image was taken from a distance of 60 km using Hera's monochromatic Asteroid Framing Camera, which captures images in black and white.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The European Space Agency's (ESA) Hera spacecraft has captured its first close-up image of the Didymos asteroid system, offering scientists a surprising new perspective on the site of NASA's historic asteroid deflection experiment.

On September 26, 2022, NASA's DART spacecraft deliberately crashed into Dimorphos, the smaller of the two asteroids in the system. Hera's latest image provides a look at its larger companion, Didymos, from a side that scientists had not previously seen in such detail.

The image was taken from a distance of 60 km using Hera's monochromatic Asteroid Framing Camera, which captures images in black and white. Although most of Dimorphos, which measures 151 m across, is concealed in shadow, the much larger Didymos, with a diameter of 780 m, is clearly visible.

A Surprisingly Different Side of Asteroid Didymos.

"The first thing we remarked was wow!" observes Hera Principal Investigator Patrick Michel, Director of Research at CNRS / Observatoire de la Côte d'Azur. "This is the other side of Didymos from the one that DART's camera showed us shortly before impact, so this feels like looking at a whole newly introduced world.

"This side of Didymos has the same central ridge along its equator that we saw before, but otherwise appears very different, with multiple boulders and craters and what look like patterns of grooves or ridges.".

The newly revealed terrain raises intriguing questions about how the asteroid's surface developed and whether NASA's collision with Dimorphos may have left traces on its larger neighbor.

Sources indicate that when DART struck Dimorphos, the impact sent material flying into space. Scientists believe some of that debris may have traveled across the roughly 1 km separating the two asteroids and reached Didymos. Determining whether this material contributed to the features now visible on its surface will be an important part of Hera's investigation.

ESA's Hera mission scientist Michael Kueppers adds: "Since we expect a lot of impact-ejected material to have made it across the approximately 1 km of space from Dimorphos to Didymos, it may be that some of these characteristics originate from this transport of material, and we have exciting work ahead of us to sort it out. We look forward to seeing much more of both bodies and systemically mapping all the changes we identify.".

NASA's DART Mission Changed an Asteroid's Orbit.

Although Dimorphos is largely obscured in Hera's newly introduced image, it holds a remarkable place in space exploration history. It became the first object in the Solar System to have its orbit measurably altered by human activity.

Recent findings suggest that NASA achieved this milestone by sending the 580 kg DART spacecraft into Dimorphos at approximately 6.1 km/s. The collision reduced the time the smaller asteroid takes to complete an orbit around Didymos by about 33 minutes, give or take a minute. That change was substantially greater than scientists had anticipated.

According to recent reports, the experiment demonstrated that striking an asteroid with a spacecraft can change its motion through space. This approach, known as kinetic impact deflection, could potentially be used to redirect a dangerous asteroid before it reaches Earth.

Hera Begins Its Investigation of NASA's Asteroid Impact.

Industry observers note that after a two-year journey, Hera has reached the double asteroid system, located 196.8 million km from Earth. The spacecraft is now preparing for a detailed 'crash site investigation' to examine the consequences of NASA's groundbreaking experiment.

While DART demonstrated that an asteroid's orbit could be changed through a deliberate collision, Hera will help scientists understand the physical processes behind the result. By examining both asteroids and documenting their characteristics, researchers hope to improve their ability to predict how future asteroid deflection attempts might work.

Industry observers note that the findings could help transform kinetic impact deflection from a successful one-time demonstration into a dependable, repeatable planetary defense technique. Such a capability could prove critical if an asteroid were ever discovered on a collision course with Earth.

Industry observers note that "Seeing this image is a hugely exciting moment for the whole Hera family," comments Hera mission manager Ian Carnelli. "It has taken years of hard work and dedication to reach this point - but we're motivated to know that the adventure is only beginning!".

The mission's next major reveal is scheduled for November 25, when detailed images of both Didymos and Dimorphos will be unveiled, giving scientists and the public a closer look at the asteroids involved in humanity's first successful asteroid deflection experiment.

Latest Update: New discovery reveals what may be holding back room-temperature superconductors

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1011 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that imagine trains floating above their tracks, energy storage systems that waste almost no electricity, and quantum computers operating with extraordinary efficiency.
  • Now, researchers from Utrecht, Leiden, and Munich have uncovered an important clue about how superconductivity might eventually work at room temperature.
  • Industry observers note that to understand why this matters, consider something as ordinary as a toaster.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that imagine trains floating above their tracks, energy storage systems that waste almost no electricity, and quantum computers operating with extraordinary efficiency. Superconductivity could help make these technologies possible, but a major challenge has stood in the way for more than a century. Most superconducting materials function only when cooled to extremely low temperatures, making widespread use costly and complicated.

Now, researchers from Utrecht, Leiden, and Munich have uncovered an important clue about how superconductivity might eventually work at room temperature. Their findings, published in the journal Science, reveal that one of the essential requirements for superconductivity can already be satisfied without extreme cooling. The discovery offers a promising newly introduced direction in the search for materials that conduct electricity without resistance.

Industry observers note that to understand why this matters, consider something as ordinary as a toaster. When electricity passes through its metal heating element, electrical resistance causes the wire to heat up and glow red, producing the heat needed to toast bread.

Recent findings suggest that that resistance is useful for cooking, but in most electrical systems, it creates unwanted energy losses. Even something as simple as charging a phone involves some electricity being converted into heat rather than being put to useful work.

Why Superconductivity Requires Extreme Cold.

It has been revealed that superconductivity eliminates this problem by allowing electrical current to move through certain materials with zero resistance. In principle, this could dramatically improve the efficiency of electrical systems and enable technologies that are difficult or expensive to operate today.

Recent findings suggest that the challenge is temperature. Many superconductors must be cooled to approximately -260°C using liquid helium before they exhibit this remarkable behavior. Maintaining such extreme conditions requires substantial energy and expensive cooling equipment, limiting practical applications.

Recent findings suggest that superconductivity was first observed in 1911. Decades later, in the mid-1980s, researchers discovered a new class of materials that could become superconducting at much warmer temperatures, around -173°C. Although still extremely cold, this represented an important advance.

However, these materials introduced a major scientific mystery. The established theory that successfully describes conventional, low-temperature superconductivity could not explain how the newer materials worked. Despite decades of research, the mechanisms behind high-temperature superconductivity remain poorly understood.

"We don't understand superconductivity at these higher temperatures at all," claims Ingmar Swart [LINK], one of the research leaders. "And if you don't understand it, you can't systematically search for materials that become superconducting at room temperature, which is ultimately our goal.".

A Crucial Ingredient Works at Room Temperature.

According to recent reports, the new study provides an important piece of the puzzle. Swart and his colleagues have demonstrated that one of the two fundamental conditions needed for superconductivity can exist even at room temperature.

"This is really good news," notes Swart. "We show that one of the two key conditions for superconductivity can be met at room temperature. If that weren't possible, room-temperature superconductivity would be out of reach altogether.".

The finding suggests that scientists may need to focus less on whether electrons can form the necessary connections and more on how those electrons coordinate their behavior.

The Secret Lies in How Electrons Move Together.

Recent findings suggest that superconductivity depends on two essential processes. First, electrons must join together in pairs called Cooper pairs. Second, those pairs must move in a coordinated way, maintaining a shared quantum state that allows electrical current to flow without resistance.

An analogy is a dance floor filled with ten couples. Having each couple dance together is only the first step. For the entire group to move as one, all ten couples must also coordinate their movements.

Industry observers note that in conventional superconductors, electron pairing and this collective coordination emerge at the same temperature. The newly introduced findings show that high-temperature superconductors behave differently. Their electrons can form pairs at temperatures substantially higher than those needed for superconductivity itself to appear.

Even more remarkably, the researchers found that these pairs can remain intact at room temperature.

Industry observers note that "The 'glue' that holds the pairs together is strong enough to keep them together even at room temperature," says Swart. "This suggests that the second key ingredient, phase coherence, is the bottleneck.".

Recent findings suggest that phase coherence describes the coordinated quantum behavior of the electron pairs. Without it, the pairs may exist, but the material does not become superconducting. This suggests that achieving and maintaining that coordination could be the crucial remaining challenge.

"If we understand phase coherence, it may point to a path toward superconductivity at higher temperatures.".

Swart intends to investigate this process in future research, with the goal of understanding how superconductivity might be sustained at increasingly warmer temperatures.

New Technology Reveals a Hidden Superconductivity Clue.

The breakthrough was made possible by specialized measurement equipment designed and constructed by the research team.

In a recent development, unlike conventional measurement approaches, the new instruments could distinguish electrical current flowing through individual electrons from current carried by paired electrons. This allowed the researchers to examine when electron pairs formed and how they behaved inside the material.

By separating these two contributions, the team gained a clearer picture of the processes underlying high-temperature superconductivity and identified where a critical obstacle may lie.

Recent findings suggest that the findings do not mean that room-temperature superconductivity has been achieved. They do, however, demonstrate that one of its essential ingredients can survive under everyday temperature conditions. Understanding how to make those electron pairs act together could bring scientists closer to a long-sought breakthrough in electrical technology.

STARBASE, Texas  — I just finished covering the Starship Flight 15 mission, and SpaceXs incredible launch tower catch of the returned Ship 42 spacecraft isn't the only thing over the weekend that left me speechless.

In a recent development, the morning of the launch (Nov. 13), SpaceX invited media on a tour of Starbase's Starfactory facility, where it manufactures and assembles both stages of its massive Starship rocket - an unprecedented behind-the-scenes look at the production and scale of SpaceX's operations, and a glimpse of things to come as Starship notches more and more milestones the more it flies.

Sources indicate that for some context, the five-story-tall Starfactory spans approximately 1 million square feet (~93,000 meters), with operations split between Starship's Super Heavy boosters and upper stage Ships, and nearly 330,000 additional square feet (30,000 square meters) of office space. SpaceX officials describe its design as one more akin to an automotive manufacturing plant than that of a typical aerospace production site, and inside, it is absolutely alive with activity.

We entered through an arch-covered doorway underneath the giant "X" sign on the building's shorter face. Our media gaggle was met with curious glances as we were shown through the doors and guided onto the factory floor - few are ever able to cross that threshold outside of SpaceX employees, and our presence seemed as novel to those busy working as it was to us.

According to recent reports, inside, we were struck with the sheer enormity of Starship's scale. Giant stainless-steel rocket parts were meticulously scattered across different subassembly stations throughout the building, with Ship nose cones, cylindrical sections and booster components all under various stages of manufacture. The sheer quantity of the hardware was staggering, and being so close to each as we walked Starfactory's throughways was an eye-opener.

Starbase is a unique partnership of privately-owned SpaceX property and publicly-accessible land and shoreline, which has created the unique ability for anyone with a mind to do so to drive right up to the the Starship launch pad to see the facilities up close (within a few hundred feet or so, which, as rockets go, is very, very close).

Fully stacked, Starship stands more than 400 feet (120 meters) tall. Standing next to such a towering colossus on the pad is enough to drive home just how big the launch vehicle is, but standing next its segmented components inside Starfactory is even more humbling; like seeing one of Ship's upper aerodynamic flaps, which are each large enough when laid flat that you could park a pair of large SUVs on their faces with room to spare.

Starbase, Texas https://t.co/NqDWwUZXv9August 25, 2025.

As our tour continued and we passed rows of nose cones under preparation for integration, numbering as high as Ship 51, one stood out from the others. In the distance, only visible for moment between the overlapping views of other Ships as we walked through the production stations, was a nose cone with a series of windows cut out of its face - undoubtedly a prototype for, or possibly even the final article that will be used as NASA's Artemis lunar lander.

NASA has contracted SpaceX to develop a version of Starship capable of landing astronauts on the moon as a part of the agency's Artemis program, and this appeared to the Ship being readied for when that mission arrives. NASA is targeting Artemis IV as the program's first crewed lunar landing in 2028, and while the decision solidifying Starship as the lander tasked with that mission isn't finalized (Blue Origin is also vying for that spot with its Blue Moon lander), SpaceX is clearly operating with the intention of coming out ahead.

But Artemis is clearly not SpaceX's only focus, as evident by the many, many other Ships in production that did not have window holes carved out of them.SpaceX officials noted the company is at the moment completing about one Ship upper stage every two weeks, and one Super Heavy booster every four weeks, with overlapping production allowing multiple rockets to move through the factory simultaneously. The majority of the vehicles currently being assembled will carry stacks of SpaceX's upgraded Starlink Version 3 (V3) satellites.

In a recent development, the company's Starlink network in low Earth orbit currently consists of more than 11,000 spacecraft beaming wireless internet to SpaceX customers across the globe. All of those were released on SpaceX's workhorse Falcon 9 rocket, with the exception of a few more than 50 delivered on Starship's two most recent test flights. Both carried V3 Starlink stacks to add to the constellation, which SpaceX officials say each added the data capacity equivalent to ten Falcon 9 Starlink releases. And, as they fine tune Starship's design, SpaceX looks to increase the vehicle's launch cadence dramatically, growing the Starlink network as it does.

SpaceX CEO Elon Musk has stated the tech giant hopes to launch Starship about once a week beginning in 2027, and with the number of Ships we saw lined up inside Starfactory, launch vehicle inventory doesn't seem like it will be to blame if that goal isn't realized.

It has been revealed that spaceX has adopted a manufacturing process modeled after the automotive industry, where efficiency and reproduction allow for the manufacture of large numbers of identical parts. Automation is a critical part of that process, but not one SpaceX is ready to entirely rely on.

Much of the equipment and tools being used for Starship's production were designed by SpaceX engineers, who are constantly refining production processes to eliminate bottlenecks. And SpaceX has deliberately kept technicians on the floor as Starship's design continues to evolve, rather than automating procedures that might soon become obsolete.

Our tour guide compared SpaceX's manufacturing consistency goals to that of Lego bricks, which are famously precise in their production down to the micro-millimeter accuracy of what now number more than 1 trillion bricks made since the toy manufacturer began in the 1940s.

Exiting the far side of the building, we stood in the shadow of SpaceX's two towering Mega Bays, where the sections of Starship are stacked and integrated with their engines - there's one hanger for Ship, and another for Super Heavy. Each can hold about five or six assemblies, and housed two or three vehicles at the time our tour was brought by.

Recent findings suggest that both Mega Bays, however, looked small against the adjacent Gigabay SpaceX is at the moment constructing. At approximately 700,000 square feet (65,000 square meters), Gigabay will be equipped with room to accommodate up to 24 vehicles at a time, and will facilitate a major increase in SpaceX's ability to assemble its Ship and Super Heavy rockets.

In a recent development, part of SpaceX's goal with Starship is to make all of what we got to see completely routine; to make rocket introduces and landings as ordinary as commercial airline flights. Still, standing inside Starfactory, surrounded on all sides by huge spacecraft in various stages of assembly, it was hard to imagine a reality where giant rockets flying to and from space on a regular basis wouldn't feel like science fiction.

Sources indicate that later that day a giant rocket introduced to outer space - Super Heavy did attempt a return to pad, but was diverted for an offshore landing instead, where it exploded. But the next day, Ship 42 came plunging through the overcast cloud cover, falling belly-first toward the same tower it left just a couple dozen hours before. And then it lit its engines and was caught by the tower.

That felt like science fiction too.

Sources indicate that josh Dinner is Space.com's Spaceflight Staff Writer and a photographer with a passion for science and exploration. He has worked the space beat since 2016, covering the evolution of NASA's commercial spaceflight partnerships and crewed missions, planetary science missions, the Artemis program and humanity's return to the moon. He also enjoys building 1:144-scale model rockets and spacecraft. Find some of Josh's launch photography on Instagram, and follow him on X, where he mostly posts in haiku.

‘Home Alone’ Director Chris Columbus Mentioned Minutes Before Fresh Sequel Was Announced That Another Movie ‘Can’t Happen’ After Catherine O’Hara’s Death

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (672 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Variety

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Chris Columbus didn’t know a latest “Home Alone” was coming.
  • The director of the 1990 original spoke with Variety minutes before news broke that Disney is developing a new installment with Macaulay Culkin.
  • “Catherine, as I’ve always noted, is 50% of ‘Home Alone,’” Columbus states.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Chris Columbus didn’t know a latest “Home Alone” was coming.

The director of the 1990 original spoke with Variety minutes before news broke that Disney is developing a new installment with Macaulay Culkin. According to sources, Columbus had no knowledge that the project was in development or about to be announced. When asked about the franchise’s future, his answer was that any return faces a steep climb without Catherine O’Hara. Related Stories Documentary 'Porno Para Ricardo,' About Cuban Punk Musician Gorki, Reveals 'the Struggle of a Free Spirit Trapped in a Cage' Peter Alsted’s Animal Conservation Doc ‘Dr. Hedgehog’ Boarded by Autlook Filmsales Ahead of IDFA Forum (EXCLUSIVE).

“Catherine, as I’ve always noted, is 50% of ‘Home Alone,’” Columbus states. “There’s the yin and yang of ‘Home Alone’: Catherine O’Hara and Macaulay Culkin. Without those two in the film, there is no film, because they create the emotional epicenter of that film.”.

O’Hara, who played Kevin McCallister’s mother, Kate, died Jan. 30 at 71.

As reported Friday, Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg are shaping the script with Culkin and will produce through their Point Grey banner. The project is in early development at Disney, and plot details and casting remain under wraps. According to Deadline, the film grew out of a pitch Culkin made to Disney film chief David Greenbaum, told from the point of view of an older Kevin as a father.

When Variety followed up after the announcement, Columbus declined to comment further.

Columbus, who is set to receive a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame in December, was particularly warm about his former star’s return to the role in a McDonald’s holiday commercial released Nov. 17. “I love Macaulay’s McDonald’s commercial,” he says. “Macaulay is a great actor, and I hope to work with him on something. Maybe it’ll be ‘Home Alone’-related, maybe it won’t.”.

He leaves the door open to a return built around the original ensemble.

“I think you potentially could still entertain the idea of doing another ‘Home Alone’ with the cast,” Columbus explains. “Not any of these ridiculous follow-ups to the first. And I only say ridiculous because it’s weird with filmmakers. They don’t understand why that cast works so well. It’s always about the cast. It’s like ‘The Goonies.’ It’s about the cast.”.

The franchise continued without Culkin and Columbus in “Home Alone 3” (1997), “Home Alone 4” (2002), “Home Alone: The Holiday Heist” (2012) and Disney+’s “Home Sweet Home Alone” (2021).

In a recent development, but Columbus indicates O’Hara’s death has changed what a reunion could be. “It was really about Catherine and Macaulay, if anyone ever wanted to do a sequel,” he says, “and unfortunately that can’t happen now.”.

He also makes the case for the film’s burglars, Harry and Marv, played by Joe Pesci and Daniel Stern.

Sources indicate that “Let’s not downsize Harry and Marv,” Columbus says. “Daniel Stern and Joe Pesci are the ultimate comic duo for that particular film. Everyone has tried in subsequent sequels to be as funny or as interesting as Dan and Joe, and they just had a chemistry that is undefinable. So you can’t do that.”.

Industry observers note that columbus, who also directed 1992’s “Home Alone 2: Lost in Fresh York,” has long been skeptical of revisiting the property. In 2020, he told Insider that Disney’s planned reboot was “a waste of time” and that “nobody got in touch with me about it.” That project became “Home Sweet Home Alone.” Last year, he told Entertainment Tonight that another “Home Alone” would be a “mistake.”.

Rogen also has a personal connection to O’Hara. She played studio executive Patty Leigh in his Apple TV comedy “The Studio,” a role she still held when she died. O’Hara also spoke at Culkin’s own Walk of Fame ceremony in December 2023.

Columbus is next set to direct “Gremlins 3,” which is scheduled to begin shooting early next year. He executive produced Robert Eggers’ upcoming horror film “Werwulf,” which Focus Features opens Dec. 25.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In late January, Amazon‘s Brett Ratner-directed Melania documentary debuted at the Kennedy Center in Washington amid crowds of demonstrators in the wake of the fatal shootings by ICE agents of Alex Pretti and Renée Good in Minneapolis. The president had also sparked backlash for his efforts to overhaul the Kennedy Center, including adding his name to the exterior, which are still playing out in court.

Industry observers note that thursday night, Melania: The Series, a two-episode follow-up, though part of the initial $40 million project, consisting of bonus footage, debuted at Latest York’s Lincoln Center. Those involved with the film and series downplayed any significance of the change in venue, noting the president and first lady’s ties to New York. But if there were demonstrators, they weren’t seen or heard by those inside the tight-security screening at Alice Tully Hall, though whether that’s due to people moving on or the premiere location remains an open question. Related Stories Business Trump's $15 Billion Defamation Suit Against The New York Times Moves Forward TV CBS Inks New Deal to Air Kennedy Center Honors.

The screening came just two weeks after the 2026 midterm elections saw Democrats score historic, surprise victories in a referendum on the president that will result in a change in party control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate.

Still, Trump’s longtime adviser Marc Beckman previously teased that the docuseries, now streaming on Amazon’s Prime Video, would be a “total different experience, completely latest.”.

Speaking to The Hollywood Reporter ahead of the Melania: The Series premiere, Beckman explained how the filmmaking team determined what would go in the documentary and what would be for the series.

Sources indicate that “We decided that we would bifurcate and isolate certain stories that we thought were suitable for the series that weren’t necessarily appropriate for the film,” Beckman mentioned. “The reason they’re suitable for the series is because it gives us more time to unpack more of her storyline, more about her family, more about her career, more about philanthropy and also what happens right after the inauguration when she takes on the role of being first lady of the United States again.”.

Melania: The Series producer Fernando Sulichin, who took on the same role on the documentary, added that the film “was about going into the inauguration, and this one is first lady in action and what she’s about, more intimate — not the preparation of becoming the first lady but being the first lady.”.

Beckman likened the approach to what Trump’s team did with her 2024 self-titled memoir Melania.

“With the trade edition of the book, we tell the story and we have certain photos in it, and then the collector’s edition, it’s a completely different experience so the fans could get both and enjoy them,” he said. “That’s the same thing here.”.

Though it was initially expected that the docuseries would arrive on Amazon’s Prime Video when the documentary began streaming in March, Beckman remarked that was “just the media speculating,” and insisted the timing of the series’ release was in keeping with the licensing deal with Amazon he negotiated for the film and series.

“The timing for the contract is exactly what we’ve done,” he told THR on the black carpet Thursday night. “I negotiated the contract, so trust me, there’s no delay.”.

While the documentary film, which was released in theaters in late January, followed Trump in the two weeks leading up to the start of her husband’s second term as president, the docuseries, in which Trump answers softball questions about her daily routine, interests and beliefs, first focuses on her role as a wife and mother, including her relationship with the president, followed by an episode centered around her and the president’s trips to North Carolina in the wake of Hurricane Helene and Los Angeles after the 2025 wildfires.

The film, coming in the wake of Trump’s best-selling memoir, was seen as part of a launch of a lifestyle brand. The doc and series’ $40 million Amazon purchase sparked backlash that the tech giant was trying to curry favor with the White House, criticism likely to continue with the project’s latest extension.

And while the Lincoln Center screening boasted Trump’s signature black-and-white color palette, complete with a black carpet and white tables and flowers, as well as tickets and popcorn boxes featuring the first lady’s face, Beckman steered questions about a possible lifestyle manufacturer back to Trump’s humanitarian efforts, specifically her work brokering a ceasefire in Oleshky, Ukraine and her Fostering the Future initiative to provide resources and educational opportunities for foster kids.

“I think right now what she’s really proud of is how she’s helping children and people throughout the world,” Beckman said. “What she’s doing in America is so much more important than a lifestyle brand.”.

And before the docuseries premiered, Trump spoke, from a black-and-white podium bearing her name, about the Ukraine ceasefire, connecting it to her own personal ethos and the series’ focus, and episode titles, of “Family & Trust” and “Pride & Honor.”.

Industry observers note that “We live in a world that never stops moving, but life’s greatest moments belong to those who can stand still,” she began. “In calmness, we can see beauty. In peace, we can see humanity. My work is demanding, and sometimes the challenges I face seem impossible. Still, even in the most difficult circumstances, I find the drive to achieve the impossible. I rely on my own strength and character, with conviction, courage and reckless determination. I found a way forward where others would not.”.

Sources indicate that “For a brief moment, the world stood still for Oleshky. Eight hundred lives were saved. After so many years of fighting, the ceasefire brought a little bit of sunshine into lives which had been in the shadows of fear and war. The moment was very powerful for me because fighting and conflict have no value to the families on either side. Peace is rational,” she continued. “In the Oleshky ceasefire, we see the power of family, the restoration of trust and the courage of young children who do not back down in the face of war. Family, trust, pride, honor are the values we all hold in our hearts; they are also the foundation of the personal story I’m going to share with you tonight as part of Melania: The Series.”.

As Trump teased that the series offered the opportunity to “experience [her] world through a latest lens,” Trump’s current and former colleagues said they hoped the show, like the documentary, let Trump tell her own story.

President Trump’s first-term adviser Kellyanne Conway said conceptually that the documentary and series were “so amazing.”.

It has been revealed that “She’s obviously a very private person who has a very public life and in my view a very positive impact and that story does not get told,” Conway told THR. “And that’s OK, so let her tell her own story.”.

Industry observers note that fashion designer Hervé Pierre, who created the first lady’s inaugural gowns for the president’s first and second ceremonies, added, “She’s not mysterious, but she’s not all over the media all the time and I think when she does something like she just did with [Russia and Ukraine], it’s not, like, fluff. It’s a very specific mission. So I think it’s notable. I hope we will discover something that we don’t know about her. And I think sometimes it’s better for her to [express something in her own words] than to have an interpretation of what she’s doing. At least you have a direct line.”.

And what sort of things might viewers discover about Trump that they don’t already know?

Pierre, who’s long worked with the first lady, offered a couple of insights.

Sources indicate that “She cries when she laughs,” he mentioned of her tendency to tear up at humorous moments. “She’s very happy. I’ve worked with difficult women for 30 years in haute couture. She never, ever raised her voice or [had attitude]. She’s always in a good mood — it’s fascinating.”.

#24700. Latest Update: More than a billion years of Earth's history vanished. Scientists may finally know why

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1109 w)

Latest Update: More than a billion years of Earth's history vanished. Scientists may finally know why

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1109 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that more than a billion years of Earth's geological history are missing from some of the planet's rock formations.
  • According to recent reports, A study led by a PhD candidate at the University of Wollongong (UOW) offers a upcoming explanation for the Great Unconformity, one of geology's most enduring mysteries.
  • Lead author Santosh Dhungana, a UOW PhD candidate, explained that although researchers have proposed numerous explanations for the Great Unconformity, few have been rigorously tested against the long-term behavior of Earth's interior.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that more than a billion years of Earth's geological history are missing from some of the planet's rock formations. Scientists have debated the cause of this enormous gap for decades, but fresh research suggests that the answer may lie in the slow movement of entire continents, driven by powerful forces deep inside Earth.

According to recent reports, A study led by a PhD candidate at the University of Wollongong (UOW) offers a upcoming explanation for the Great Unconformity, one of geology's most enduring mysteries. Published in the journal Nature, the findings suggest that ancient continents gradually rose and sank over hundreds of millions of years as hot rock moved through Earth's interior. These changes in elevation may have allowed erosion to remove enormous amounts of rock, erasing vast stretches of the planet's geological record.

Lead author Santosh Dhungana, a UOW PhD candidate, explained that although researchers have proposed numerous explanations for the Great Unconformity, few have been rigorously tested against the long-term behavior of Earth's interior.

Sources indicate that "Imagine a book where a huge section in the middle has been ripped out. The Great Unconformity is that gap in Earth's story, with the narrative jumping from the early chapters straight to a much later part of the story. Our research suggests these pages weren't lost by chance," he noted.

Earth's Mysterious Missing Billion Years.

Industry observers note that normally, layers of sedimentary rock accumulate over time, creating a geological timeline in which older rocks lie beneath younger ones. Scientists can study these layers to reconstruct ancient environments and understand how Earth has changed over billions of years.

Yet this timeline contains a remarkable interruption. At numerous locations worldwide, sedimentary rocks dating to the Cambrian period, around 540 million years ago, rest directly on much older crystalline rocks, including granite that can be more than a billion years old. The intervening geological layers are absent, leaving an enormous break in the record known as the Great Unconformity.

One of the clearest examples is visible in the Grand Canyon in the United States. This region was once part of Laurentia (modern North America), an ancient continental landmass. Similar gaps have been identified in Europe, Australia, Africa and Asia.

In a recent development, the amount of missing time varies considerably between locations. In some places, approximately 200 million years of geological history are absent, while elsewhere the gap exceeds a billion years.

How Forces Deep Inside Earth May Have Erased the Rock Record.

To investigate what caused these missing chapters, Dhungana worked with his supervisor and co-author, Associate Professor Nicolas Flament, to simulate the movement of Earth's mantle over hundreds of millions of years.

According to recent reports, the mantle is an immense layer of hot, mostly solid rock beneath Earth's crust. Although this material appears rigid on human timescales, it can deform and flow extremely slowly over geological periods. Heat-driven circulation within the mantle, a process called mantle convection, can gradually raise enormous regions of Earth's surface or cause them to subside.

According to recent reports, these vertical movements can influence whether ancient rocks are exposed to erosion or buried beneath upcoming deposits. When a continent rises, wind, water and other natural processes can gradually wear away its surface. If the land later sinks, oceans can advance over it, allowing fresh sediment to accumulate on top of the eroded rock.

The researchers found that this process may explain both the disappearance of ancient rock layers and the preservation of the geological boundary that remains visible today.

Ancient Continents Rose and Sank Over Millions of Years.

The simulations revealed a striking pattern across three major ancient continental regions: Laurentia, Baltica (northern Europe) and North China.

According to the models, mantle convection caused the ancient cores of these continents to rise during the Neoproterozoic Era, which extended from roughly one billion to 540 million years ago. This long interval preceded the Cambrian period, when animal life underwent a remarkable expansion in diversity, commonly known as the Cambrian explosion.

As the continents remained elevated, prolonged erosion could have stripped away extensive layers of older rock, gradually removing hundreds of millions of years of geological history.

The researchers found that this period of uplift was followed by widespread subsidence during the Phanerozoic eon, which encompasses approximately the past 540 million years. As these ancient continental regions slowly sank, advancing seas covered their eroded surfaces. New sediments accumulated above the exposed older rocks, preserving the boundary between the two.

Over immense spans of time, this sequence of uplift, erosion, subsidence and sediment deposition could have produced the Great Unconformity seen in rock formations today.

A Upcoming Explanation for One of Earth's Greatest Geological Mysteries.

A particularly important finding was how closely the computer simulations matched the geographical distribution of the Great Unconformity.

The models predicted long-term uplift followed by subsidence in North America, northern Europe and North China, precisely the regions where the geological gap is especially well documented and preserved.

This agreement provides support for the idea that deep mantle movements played a major role in shaping the missing rock record. Rather than requiring a separate explanation for each location, the findings suggest that a common process operating deep within Earth may account for the widespread pattern.

"Sometimes what is missing can tell us more about the story of Earth than what we can see. A single, long period of uplift followed by a long period of sinking would have been the ideal recipe for removing the rock and preserving the worn surface," Associate Professor Flament stated.

In a recent development, the research offers a way to connect the geological evidence visible at Earth's surface with the slow processes occurring far below it. Although the findings do not establish that mantle convection was the only factor responsible for the Great Unconformity, they provide a testable explanation for why so much ancient geological history disappeared and how the remaining evidence survived.

It has been revealed that "Many explanations for the Great Unconformity had been proposed but few had been tested against how the Earth actually behaves over time. It is a thrill to be able to propose a solution to this geological puzzle.".

Materials provided by University of Wollongong. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

Uganda minister at COP31: 'We need a just transition'

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (900 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ugandan Environment Minister Beatrice Atim Anywar has come to the UN climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, seeking to secure more funding for her country as it grapples with climate change.
  • "This is a thing we are living with," she told DW on the sidelines of the COP31 summit, where she's leading the Ugandan delegation.
  • In recent years, the East African nation has been hit by a series of climate-related disasters, from deadly landslides and floods washing away villages, to droughts damaging harvests and hydroelectricity production.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ugandan Environment Minister Beatrice Atim Anywar has come to the UN climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, seeking to secure more funding for her country as it grapples with climate change.

"This is a thing we are living with," she told DW on the sidelines of the COP31 summit, where she's leading the Ugandan delegation. "People are displaced, people are dying of harm, hunger. It has implications on food security and livelihoods.".

In recent years, the East African nation has been hit by a series of climate-related disasters, from deadly landslides and floods washing away villages, to droughts damaging harvests and hydroelectricity production.

"When we come to COP and we talk of what the reality is on the ground, we Ugandans have suffered it," Anywar said, referring to the effects of climate change.

"It has an implication for the health of our people, on national budgets," she added.

Recent findings suggest that climate financing for developing countries to deal with the impacts of a warming planet has become a major sticking point at this year's climate talks. The gathering of some 200 states is seeking to close gaps on how to scale up financing from developed states and whether support should be provided through grants or loans.

Africa contributes less than 4% of the global greenhouse emissions that drive rising temperatures globally, but the continent is among the most vulnerable to climate impacts.

As it deals with the affects of climate change, including extreme weather, Uganda is also rapidly expanding investment in electricity production from renewables such as hydropower and solar.

In the country of some 53 million people, more than 90% of Ugandan households still rely on wood and charcoal as the most affordable fuel for things like cooking. Biomass accounts for 90% of the country's final energy consumption.

Sources indicate that while using wood and charcoal leads to deforestation, Ugandans have little choice. Only around 2% of the country's energy comes from electricity — which is largely derived from hydropower — and less than half of the population has access to electricity.

Recent findings suggest that "Now we are deliberately going into scaling up the production of electricity — hydropower electricity — and making it cheaper for cooking," Anywar said. "We have other alternative energy sources... to mitigate this charcoal use. But the use needs to be phased out in a systematic manner by giving them alternatives.".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

At the same time, the country is seeking to boost economic development by becoming an oil producer. Due to open in 2027, a controversial 1,443-kilometer (897-mile) pipeline is nearly complete. It connects two oil sites in eastern Uganda with a port on the Tanzanian coast.

Industry observers note that environmentalists have criticized the East African Crude Oil Pipeline project, which can transport up to 246,000 barrels per day. Environmentalists say it runs counter to the goal of limiting global temperature rise and could damage fragile ecosystems.

The Climate Accountability Institute mentioned it would release 379 million tons of climate-heating pollution over its 20-year lifetime.

Oil wells for the project, operated by French energy giant TotalEnergies, are also located in Uganda's largest and oldest national park, Murchison Falls.

Industry observers note that "That has been also a sticky glitch. And actually, that is one of the challenges we are facing at COPs," Anywar said. She stressed that measures have been taken to limit emissions, and that the project was progressing in a "very deliberate way.".

The minister also urged developed countries to cut less wealthy nations some slack for using the resources they have to drive much-needed development, saying oil revenues could help fund the transition to cleaner energy.

"You cannot tell us to cut off the umbilical cord that feeds us, as much as it has to be cut off," Anywar noted, criticizing the lack of financing from developed countries to deal with climate change. "We are here begging for funds that are not forthcoming.".

Anywar added that developing countries "need a just transition," referring to an equitable shift away from fossil fuels that focuses on protecting workers and communities.

Another way Uganda is looking to finance climate change adaptation is through carbon credits, Anywar noted, describing them as a potential "breakthrough.".

Sources indicate that carbon credits are tradeable permits representing one ton of carbon dioxide that has been reduced or removed from the atmosphere through initiatives such as forest protection, renewable energy projects or tree planting schemes. Companies or governments can buy them to offset emissions they have not cut themselves.

Industry observers note that "Our country is rich with biodiversity. And that is what we are looking forward to — attracting investors into our natural setup so that we earn some finances," Anywar noted.

Carbon credits have been promoted as an crucial source of income for developing countries. But they have also faced criticism, for a lack of transparency and allowing polluting activities to continue.

"We need to have a bankable approach to all interventions. Otherwise… it's not going to work for us," Anywar remarked, adding that her country also wants to attract investment and build partnerships in smart agriculture and the energy transition.

"If we rely on begging for funds which are not forthcoming, we shall go back empty handed.".

This interview also appeared as a video.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The highest-grossing biopic ever made is sitting out one of the biggest stops on the road to the Oscars.
  • “Michael,” Antoine Fuqua’s billion-dollar portrait of the King of Pop, will not be submitted for the 2027 EE BAFTA Film Awards, Variety has learned exclusively.
  • According to sources with direct knowledge, producer Graham King, Fuqua and various stakeholders made the call after consulting with Lionsgate, international distributor Universal Pictures and the film’s other partners.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The highest-grossing biopic ever made is sitting out one of the biggest stops on the road to the Oscars.

“Michael,” Antoine Fuqua’s billion-dollar portrait of the King of Pop, will not be submitted for the 2027 EE BAFTA Film Awards, Variety has learned exclusively. That takes actors like Jaafar Jackson and Colman Domingo, along with the film’s entire craft team, out of the running before longlist voting begins. Related Stories Berlin Winner Tatiana Huezo Close to Completing Road Movie ‘Galerna’ Following Awards Boost: ‘I’m Dying to Finish It’ 'The Year of the Ghost,' About Misogyny in China, Wins Best Film at IDFA Documentary Festival.

According to sources with direct knowledge, producer Graham King, Fuqua and various stakeholders made the call after consulting with Lionsgate, international distributor Universal Pictures and the film’s other partners. The sources cite “multiple factors” behind the decision but declined to say what they are.

Representatives for Lionsgate, Universal Pictures and GK Films declined to comment.

Sources tell Variety that Lionsgate and Universal supports the filmmakers’ decision.

It has been revealed that earlier this month, the organization sent film voting members its Recommended Viewing Groups for the 2027 awards, which divides every entered film into 15 groups. Each member is randomly assigned one. The British Academy encourages voters to watch as many entries as they can but asks those short on time to prioritize their assigned group and the films in their specialist craft category. “Michael” isn’t in any of them.

It has been revealed that BAFTA’s Stage Two entry and deadline passed Nov. 19. A draft list of entered films goes out to entrants and members Nov. 26. The final list will be published on Dec. 4, the same morning Round One voting opens to set the longlists.

Among the films that entered are “The Odyssey,” “Artificial,” “Behemoth!,” “Project Hail Mary,” “Wuthering Heights” and “The Social Reckoning.” The year’s other box office heavyweights, “The Super Mario Galaxy Movie” and “Spider-Man: Brand Upcoming Day,” are also in the mix, along with two music documentaries, “Epic: Elvis Presley in Concert” and “Oasis: Don’t Look Back in Anger.”.

It’s an unusual move for a film that has spent the fall building an awards case.

Recent findings suggest that the 80th BAFTA Film Awards reclaim its traditional spot ahead of the Academy this season. Last year, the British Academy announced nominations five days after the Oscars did, breaking a pattern that had held since 2001. This time, longlists arrive Jan. 7 and nominations Jan. 19, two days before the Academy unveils its own on Jan. 21. The London ceremony follows Feb. 21, three weeks ahead of the March 14 Oscars at the Dolby Theatre. For voters on both sides of the Atlantic, the BAFTA ballot is the first real read on the Oscar race, especially given the Academy’s large international voting bloc.

It has been revealed that it’s also a departure from producer King’s own playbook. “Bohemian Rhapsody,” his last music biopic, won Rami Malek the BAFTA for leading actor on the way to four Oscars, which he repeated.

Sources indicate that king has criticized the British Academy before. After February’s ceremony, Tourette’s syndrome campaigner John Davidson involuntarily shouted the N-word while “Sinners” stars Michael B. Jordan and Delroy Lindo presented the night’s first award, and the BBC aired the slur despite a two-hour tape delay. Both organizations apologized.

Sources indicate that “For years, BAFTA and the BBC have repeatedly displayed cultural insensitivity and tone deafness,” King said at the time in a statement posted to his GK Films’ Instagram account. “Their inability to take accountability for their actions or inactions is reckless and unacceptable.”.

The sources did not say whether the episode factored into this year’s decision.

Recent findings suggest that the news also comes after the Golden Globes rejected the studio’s bid to place “Michael” in the comedy or musical categories, a submission that came with a letter from Fuqua, pushing the film into the more crowded drama race. An FYC screening at the DGA reportedly drew a standing ovation.

It has been revealed that at the Gotham Awards on Nov. 30, Fuqua, King, Jaafar Jackson, Colman Domingo and Nia Long will accept the Musical Tribute Award.

The commercial case was settled months ago, with a sequel currently in development.

Sources indicate that “Michael” opened in April to $97 million domestically and $217 million worldwide, a record debut for a music biopic. In July, it became the first biopic to cross $1 billion globally. It’s Lionsgate’s biggest release ever, topping the $865 million of “The Hunger Games: Catching Fire” and the studio indicates it’s the first film from an independent distributor to reach the milestone.

According to recent reports, the critics’ reception was much harsher than audiences’. The film at the moment holds a 38% score on Rotten Tomatoes. However, viewers have consistently singled out Jaafar Jackson’s star-making turn as his uncle; audiences gave it an A- CinemaScore.

Industry observers note that written by John Logan, “Michael” traces Jackson’s rise from the Jackson 5 in the 1960s through the Bad World Tour in the late 1980s, closing before the first allegations of misconduct became public in 1993. Jaafar Jackson leads a cast that includes Domingo as Joseph Jackson, Long as Katherine Jackson, Miles Teller as attorney John Branca and Mike Myers as record executive Walter Yetnikoff.

Skipping BAFTA doesn’t affect the film’s Oscar eligibility, and the Globes, Critics Choice Awards and guild circuits remain in play. But it gives up one of the season’s biggest televised platforms, along with one of the few chances for a breakout performance to reach an international voting body before Oscar nominations voting opens.

Whether the decision ultimately costs “Michael” a trip to the Oscars remains to be seen.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Political advertisers spent a record $12.06 billion during the 2025-26 elections, making it the first time a midterm cycle outspent a presidential cycle, according to a report from advertising intelligence organization AdImpact released Tuesday.
  • Total spending exceeded AdImpact's June projection by more than $460 million.
  • The elections also marked the first time in over a decade that Republicans have outspent Democrats on advertisements, according to AdImpact.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Political advertisers spent a record $12.06 billion during the 2025-26 elections, making it the first time a midterm cycle outspent a presidential cycle, according to a report from advertising intelligence organization AdImpact released Tuesday.

Total spending exceeded AdImpact's June projection by more than $460 million.

The elections also marked the first time in over a decade that Republicans have outspent Democrats on advertisements, according to AdImpact.

Despite Republicans leading spending, John Link, senior vice president of data at AdImpact, noted that "Dems still led or were generally even with overall airings and impressions.".

The record spending extended across the board, with every type of race reaching a new high. Senate spending hit $3.39 billion, while spending on gubernatorial elections reached $2.61 billion, spending on races in the House of Representatives grew to $2.44 billion and state legislative races totaled $602 million, all records, according to AdImpact.

The 2026 midterm cycle was largely powered by megadonors, with SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk becoming the largest contributor by funneling more than $366 million into campaigns.

In a recent development, the biggest donors in this year's election disproportionately favored Republicans, according to a CNBC analysis of Federal Election Commission records. Fourteen out of the 20 largest donor groups supported GOP candidates, according to that analysis.

Republicans spent $5.51 billion on political advertisements, compared with $5.11 billion spent by Democrats, according to AdImpact.

While Republican spending increased by 27% from 2024, spending by Democrats fell by 4%.

Fundraisers told CNBC in interviews that Democratic donors' hesitancy largely stems from memories of Kamala Harris' defeat in 2024, unease about the rise of democratic socialism and distrust in party leadership.

Though they were outspent, Democrats made sweeping gains against Republicans in races nationwide, taking control of both the House and the Senate and flipping seats in some of the most competitive places, including Texas and Kansas.

It is not the first time spending did not align with the winners. In 2024, President Donald Trump defeated former Vice President Harris despite Democrats outspending Republicans.

While party majorities in Congress have switched hands, the most popular medium for political ads has not changed.

Broadcast television represented the largest category for spending in this year's election, accounting for 49%, or $5.85 billion, of political ad spending, according to AdImpact. Broadcast's share of political ad dollars is up slightly from 48% in 2024.

Broadcast TV's strength comes despite facing pressure from falling viewership and increasing competition from streaming.

It has been revealed that industry experts have told CNBC that political advertisers continue to spend on broadcast because it reaches local markets and active voting populations. The Associated Press also reported that airtime was so expensive during the midterm elections that some candidates, including Republican Ken Paxton in Texas, bought ads during national sporting events, figuring that reaching enough constituents through a national broadcast might actually be less expensive than buying across the state's local television markets.

The fastest-growing categories in this year's cycle were connected TV, or internet-connected devices like Apple TV or Roku, with $2.66 billion, and digital, with $1.91 billion. Both mediums grew double digits from the 2024 presidential election. Spending on cable and radio declined 7% and 13%, respectively, from 2024.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Himalayas tower below the clouds, capped in icy snow in newly introduced snapshots captured from aboard the International Space Station.

Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk was looking out one of the windows aboard the space station when the most incredible view came into focus  — and thankfully he had a camera handy and was able to capture these striking scenes of the Himalayas from space.

Above the mountain range, fluffy clouds hang in the atmosphere. Below, the expansive Himalayas are covered in bright snow and ice, which looks somehow both white and blue at the same time as the bright sunlight streaks across the breathtaking expanse.

This frosty winter scene showcases the mountain range from orbit, from about 250 miles (400 kilometers) above Earth's surface. But even from this distance, the magnitude of this mountain range is palpable. The Himalayas stretch across five different countries including Nepal, India, China, Bhutan and Pakistan. And the Himalayas include some of the highest mountain peaks on planet Earth, including Mount Everest.

Himalayas 🗻 https://t.co/IzGzu20H4QNovember 17, 2026.

From orbit around Earth, you might expect even the largest landmarks on our planet to appear miniscule. But somehow, in these photographs snapped by Kutryk during NASA's SpaceX Crew-13 mission, even from hundreds of miles above our planet you can really see and feel the immense scale of this mammoth mountain range.

It's unclear exactly where above the mountain range these photographs were taken, but it is always amazing to think that within these sweeping landscapes are people living their lives, likely unaware that an astronaut is taking in the beauty of their home.

Sources indicate that perhaps somewhere hidden under the clouds in one of Kutryk's photographs are hikers climbing up the side of Mt. Everest, completing their own bucket list adventure as the astronauts watching from above complete theirs.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • [This story contains mild spoilers from the premiere of Yellowjackets season four.].
  • Recent findings suggest that the end is near for Yellowjackets.
  • “Life just keeps getting wider, and the show has been part of that.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

[This story contains mild spoilers from the premiere of Yellowjackets season four.].

Recent findings suggest that the end is near for Yellowjackets. The fourth and final season of Showtime‘s hit survival story has begun, and the weekly drop of final episodes will send viewers on a wild ride as they ruminate on life, death — and the meanings behind those bizarre post-Yellowjackets dreams. If it’s any consolation, the creators have those dreams, too.

“Life just keeps getting wider, and the show has been part of that. It’s been an expression of that width and an agent in creating that width,” Bart Nickerson, chatting with his co-creator wife, Ashley Lyle, tells The Hollywood Reporter of the last near-decade making the hit Showtime series. The pair initially planned for five seasons, but when the Paramount renewed Yellowjackets for a fourth and final season, the creators pivoted. Related Stories NEXT SIGNIFICANT THING Jasmin Savoy Brown Bids Farewell to 'Yellowjackets' and Finds Her Way to 'Hadestown' Lifestyle The Paramount+ Black Friday Deal Gets You Two Months for Less Than a Latte.

Industry observers note that “For us,” says Lyle, “it was about storytelling momentum and, with the uncertainty of the industry right now, let’s just finish a story if we can. We took a good, hard look at it. If we had felt like we couldn’t get it done, we probably wouldn’t have taken the chance. But it felt like we could.”.

What they deliver is what viewers have been waiting for when the survivors of the Yellowjackets plane crash that began the series are rescued and returned home in the season four premiere. Following the teens as they reassimilate into life in Latest Jersey — while learning how to live with the murders and cannibalistic acts they harbor; the things they did to survive those months in the wilderness — delivers a fascinating watch and full-circle return to where this story began.

Below, Lyle and Nickerson dive into making the final season and what to expect, including the pain of killing off characters while always knowing who would survive in the end. They also explain why they aren’t interested in spinoffs — because they’re ending the story with a period, not an ellipses: “We do feel like this closes the book, and I think that’s crucial. I think that’s part of the contract with the audience — that you’re telling a complete story.”.

It has been revealed that we have been waiting for this rescue season. When we spoke with you two way back in the beginning of all of this, in your heads, you had envisioned Yellowjackets as a five-season show, and here you are ending with four seasons.

How massive of a pivot was this to wrap up the show earlier than you planned?

Sources indicate that LYLE Ultimately, as we were breaking this season, we realized that it was workable. It came down to: Do we potentially overstay our welcome? Of course, when you’re making television, there’s always a risk that you will not get another season. So we realized at a certain point that there was a much more high-octane version of this season that could accomplish all the things that we really hoped to accomplish when we first conceived of the show.

Coming off of the third season, we always knew we wanted to get the girls back home. Then we always knew in the adult timeline that we wanted things to start turning in on itself amongst these women in their relationships. And it did feel like we had hit that pivot point at the end of season three. So we just ended up going full steam ahead; burden the hand. The ability to tell a complete story, to finish it on our own terms, is something we’re incredibly grateful for. We hope everyone feels a sense of satisfaction with this final season.

Given the narrative of viewers dropping off after two seasons of a show, did you feel like season three was the hardest point to keep your audience, and did that affect what you wanted to do going into four?

Sources indicate that BART NICKERSON To be honest, I didn’t know that was a thing — that audiences drop after two season. I think, in some respect, through the entire run of the show, there is, as it turns out, a gift in being, tremendously insecure and scared. (Laughs.) Every script we’ve ever written, even if we’re just going to our writers group, you have so much of your personal self-worth and the quality of that script, you kind of live and die on every piece of feedback. Although it sounds insane, the stakes of making a season of television are almost a little intellectual — you don’t ever stand in front of the audience and hear them reacting to your thing. Because the stakes are always so high, it wasn’t about: How do we keep this going? Or: People didn’t like this, how do we address that? At the end of the day, you just have to make the story you’re trying to make for better or for worse. And some may say for worse! (Laughs.).

LYLE I don’t really understand the metrics of how they’re counting viewership at this point. I’m not sure anybody does. I think they mentioned season three was the most watched, but some of that, I’m sure, is people catching up on Netflix. For us, it was about storytelling momentum and, with the uncertainty of the industry right now, let’s just finish a story if we can. And we took a good, hard look at it. If we had felt like we couldn’t get it done, we probably would have taken the chance. But it felt like we could.

Sources indicate that as the storytellers, you have a huge ensemble. So many stories to tell. What were some of the biggest challenges knowing that this was it? That you had a finite number of episodes left.

NICKERSON Yes, just that in and of itself [is the challenge]. We love television. We love telling television stories, and we love our characters and want them all to have a full, complete arc. Then there is the reality only having so many pages and so many minutes on screen. So it’s about how to be as efficient as possible, and that has always been a challenge. We’ve always wanted each episode, each season, each scene to have a beginning, middle and an end. So it’s about, how do you tell these stories with efficiency but also arc? That has always been an incredible challenge.

Recent findings suggest that did it leave more things on the cutting room floor? Anything you can share now that didn’t work or make the show?

LYLE Not necessarily in a macro sense for this season. Every episode, we’re always over time. We’ll sit with the editors and pull out 10 seconds at a time to get it under 60 minutes. You’re always cutting. That was the case in season one. That was the case in season two. Sometimes you go back and go, “Remember when that scene existed?” And the fact is that it was sort of telling you that it didn’t need to be there. So I think the process kind of works itself out as you go.

Does it leave more room for spinoffs?

LYLE That’s a question for Paramount Skydance!

NICKERSON Having one less season [I don’t think changes that], because we came to an end that was meant to be the final end. There are always ideas you haven’t had yet. So, never say never. But there isn’t something where it’s like, because we had one last season, we could come back and revisit that.

According to recent reports, do you two feel like you are closing the Yellowjackets book with this ending? No ideas for a tangent or a right turn in any way?

Industry observers note that LYLE We do feel like this closes the book, and I think that’s crucial. I think that’s part of the contract with the audience — that you’re telling a complete story. I suppose in this day and age, there’s a never-say-never quality to this question, but at the same time, we wanted to tell a complete story. We wanted it to feel like the audience had been on the full ride. And hopefully, that there’s a lot of emotional satisfaction in the resolution that we find.

NICKERSON At the end of the day, there’s a level on which, if you’re telling a story about survival, you’re telling a story about death, and that means there has to be an end, because that’s what you’re confronting — the end-end. And, what does it mean when it’s over? I don’t think it would be possible to tell a satisfying ending if it didn’t feel like the ending … of everything … ever. (Laughs.).

It has been revealed that you come out swinging with the season four premiere jumping right into the rescue timeline. You could have built your way up to it. Can you talk about why you wanted to lead with it, and fill in the gaps from the past as the season goes?

LYLE That is a storytelling paradigm we’ve always been drawn to: not necessarily the “what happens” but the “why.” That was a massive part of season one with the question of whether or not they engage in cannibalism. There were people who noted, did you ever consider teasing that out? And we’re like, “No.” We wanted to put it in the pilot, because to us, the most interesting thing wasn’t whether or not they’d do it. It was, why did they do it? How did they get there? What is the context for it?

Industry observers note that similarly, with this season, it was a clearing of the decks, a reset in a way that could set up this season as a standalone season. And again, it wasn’t if they get rescued, it’s how and why, and what happens in the aftermath?

According to recent reports, we would talk in the writers room, now that we’ve got four timelines or (let’s just make things a little more complicated for ourselves!), in terms of post-rescue, pre-rescue and present day. And it felt like what happened in the interim between Natalie’s distress call and them getting rescued could serve much more effectively as a little bit of mystery. Because to us, the more crucial emotional heartbeat of this season was going to be the post-rescue: how they were coping with and the different ways they would personally strategize how they would handle the reintegration. That was a much more interesting question for us at this point.

Industry observers note that so much has happened to these characters over the course of the series, but it’s also been almost a decade since you two started developing this show. Do you feel like you also have grown with the show, in terms of how you wanted to end it and what you want to say in the end?

NICKERSON Speaking for myself, yes, tremendously. It would be difficult for me to fully articulate what I mean, but so much of this story is a result of stuff that’s been churned up and has continued to churned up. I always say the best compliment that people will give us about the show is, “I just started watching Yellowjackets. My dreams have been so messed up!” This idea that there is a deepness to the show.

I’ve had some bizarre dreams while watching these screeners!

NICKERSON (Laughs.) That’s been our life for nine years! Just weird dreams. (Laughs.) I feel like life just keeps getting wider, and the show has been part of that. It’s been an expression of that width and an agent in creating that width.

This show is about surviving and about death. There have been so many substantial deaths along the way. We still feel Juliette Lewis’ exit and last season, you took so many of them away! Fans are always reacting. How much did you take the fans into account when you thought about who is going to survive this season?

Recent findings suggest that LYLE We didn’t. I don’t think we can, because, ultimately, if we were trying to please some segment of the audience, we’re going to displease another. We have to write it for ourselves and use that as a guiding light and principle. It’s a fool’s errand to try to do fan service, especially when you’re planning how to end a show.

NICKERSON The first time we met with Julie Plec, who gave us our first job in television, it was a couple days after a significant character death in Vampire Diaries. It was like, “Oh, my God. I can’t believe you killed this person!” She got very serious and was like, “It’s my job to service the story before I service what the fans think they want.”.

Sources indicate that because, ultimately, when I’m rooting for a character, I have this relationship with them. I’m not really thinking about the story. I’m thinking about the character and my relationship to them. In order to give the fans something of value, you have to keep your eye on what you’re trying to build and not necessarily on how it’s going to be received.

According to recent reports, your characters are like your babies. Is there a death that still sits with you or any character you wish you still had around to play with?

Recent findings suggest that LYLE I think that speaks to what Bart was saying. They’re all difficult. But one that always comes back around as being rough for everybody involved on set was when we killed Coach Scott last season. Steven [Krueger] knew very early on — we go way, way, way back. He was like, “It’s time. I’m surprised I lasted this long.” There are moments where, man, you miss the character, you miss having that actor on set. But at the same time, it had to happen.

Sources indicate that NICKERSON And that’s one of the moments I am most proud of. Every time we watched, it was such an incredible performance by both of them [Krueger and Sophie Thatcher]. It was amazing. The whole thing to watch the Natalie character born in this ultimate sacrifice that she’s making for somebody else, but it’s also a grisly, violent act. I so miss that character. But, what are we doing if it’s not trying to create those moments?

Industry observers note that I know those calls to your departing actors have been difficult along the way, but I imagine dying in the final season is different. You probably get some cheering. It’s like a badge of honor.

LYLE It’s easier the last season!

Did you always know who would be the final girl(s), or did it change along the way?

In a recent development, NICKERSON My only hesitation is that, on the path, you investigate different things. But, no, it was at the beginning. At the beginning, this was how we were going to do it.

It has been revealed that LYLE We kicked the tires a lot. But we really ended up in the place we thought we would.

NICKERSON Yeah. Some of the particulars changed. Ultimately, the meaning of it has, for me at least, shifted. But yeah, we actually did end up where we thought we would.

I know you can’t talk spoilers. But is there anything you want to tease… will dead characters return? Will we ever see that lost episode? Any surprises in store?

According to recent reports, NICKERSON We’re not allowed to say! We want to reveal everything. We just want you to see it!

Recent findings suggest that you have always talked about having big beats you knew you wanted to hit throughout the show: Pit Girl, the scientists, rescue. Anything you can’t wait for us to see, in broad terms?

NICKERSON I don’t think it’s a spoiler to say that them coming back to New Jersey has always been a huge thing we wanted to do, and, in some sense, is the show.

LYLE There are a few things. There’s a scene in episode five that we’ve been talking about for many seasons.

NICKERSON Oh yeah, that is going to be really good! We’ve been talking about for a really long time.

According to recent reports, there have been more than one scene that made your actors unwell — and even had them throwing up. For example, the Jackie feast … the Pit Girl reveal. Was there any filming experience in this final season that’s comparable to that?

LYLE I think they toughened up a little bit.

It has been revealed that NICKERSON I mean, eating Jackie was rough. That was a tough day!

Recent findings suggest that LYLE That was really, really rough. I don’t know that we could ever top that, in terms of torturing our actors.

NICKERSON Because that thing [Jackie’s edible body] looked good. I mean, not tasty, but, oh man. Just to have what they were going to eat like around is tough.

LYLE There was a moment on set this season when Melanie [Lynskey] brought her daughter to set and sort of regretted it immediately. Like, “Oh, just kidding! Go into the trailer.” I was like, “That’s not real. It’s okay!” She seemed fine. I mean, we don’t have to pay for her therapy! (Laughs.).

Tech Report: Stonehenge’s six-ton mystery deepens as scientists narrow their search
